claims.text: With a sidecar mesh, every Pod gets a proxy, which uses memory and CPU in that Pod, and every call between services takes an extra hop through the proxies.
claims.source_hint: k8s.l4.sidecar-proxies (claims on the mesh's proxies); docs/adr/0021-chua-dung-service-mesh.md @ stage-4 lines 42-43

claims.text: A mesh's controllers (programs it runs in the cluster to hand out certificates and configure proxies) are one more platform component with the recurring work self-run-components.md names: upgrades, monitoring, someone who understands it when it breaks.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/self-run-components.md @ stage-4 lines 3-5; docs/adr/0021 @ stage-4 lines 44-45

claims.text: Because a mesh's proxies sit in every call path, one wrong mesh setting or a failed mesh upgrade can break calls between all services at once (its blast radius is every call in the cluster).
claims.source_hint: docs/adr/0021 @ stage-4 lines 46-47; k8s.l4.sidecar-proxies (every call passes through the proxies)

ADR 0021 @ stage-4 lines 32-38: options A (no mesh, P5 accepted), B (a mesh only for mTLS between all services), C (api serves HTTPS with a cert-manager certificate, Gateway calls it over HTTPS, nothing new beside Pods).

ADR 0021 @ stage-4 lines 49-70: chooses A; C is the first step if only encryption is needed; consequences: calls stay unencrypted, NetworkPolicy still decides who connects, nothing new to upgrade; three reopen conditions (contract, several teams/languages, calls across clusters).

ADR 0021 @ stage-4 lines 74-77: a backend developer asked for C now; the team declined because the api's certificate adds a renewal and a point of failure on the main entry path for a gap nobody asked to fill.

threat-model.md @ stage-4 line 72: P5 (Gateway calls api and Payments Pods over plain HTTP; api knows the caller only by address) is accepted for one cluster and one team with NetworkPolicies limiting callers, and points to ADR 0021 for reopen conditions.

claims.text: In ordinary (server-only) TLS, as in option C, only the server presents a certificate, so the api would still not know the Gateway by anything but its address; mTLS also authenticates the client.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8446 section 4.3.2 (CertificateRequest is optional; client certificate only when requested); k8s.l4.mutual-tls

claims.text: An app can serve TLS itself without a mesh: echo-mtls (Caddy with client_auth require_and_verify) did mTLS with no mesh; cert-manager can issue the certificate an app serves.
claims.source_hint: k8s.l4.mutual-tls (echo-mtls.yaml @ stage-4); cert-manager 1.20 docs: Certificate resource

claims.text: Opinion: a mesh pays off only when it buys something the team needs and lacks: a gap a requirement asks to fill, or work that would otherwise be rebuilt in every codebase. Its cost lands on every Pod and every call either way.

Opinion (the ADR's reasoning): once many services come in many languages, building mTLS, retries and per-call metrics into every codebase can cost more than a mesh; with three .NET services and one team, Đơn Hàng is not there yet.
Opinion: trade-offs table of options A, B, C on calls encrypted, caller identity, new things to run, cost per call and what one mistake can break.

Opinion: C for a contract asking only for encryption Gateway to api; a contract for more, several teams/languages or calls across clusters reopen ADR 0021; reopen before donhang-north/south calls ship, since the P5 acceptance assumed one cluster.
